module_title: Formulating Skincare Products with African Black Soap

lessons.title: Creating a Basic Black Soap Face and Body Bar
lessons.body: To make a basic black soap bar, you will need 500g of raw African black soap (crumbly or paste), 50g of shea butter, 30g of coconut oil, and 10ml of vitamin E oil (optional). You also need a double boiler, a mold (silicone or wooden), and a spatula. Start by grating or breaking the black soap into small pieces. Melt the shea butter and coconut oil in the double boiler over low heat. Once melted, add the black soap pieces and stir gently until they fully dissolve. Do not boil; high heat can destroy the soap's natural glycerin. If the mixture is too thick, add 1-2 tablespoons of warm water. Remove from heat and stir in vitamin E oil. Pour the mixture into your mold and let it cool at room temperature for 24 hours. Then unmold and cut into bars. Cure the bars on a drying rack for 1-2 weeks to harden. This recipe yields about 4-6 bars, depending on size. For a more exfoliating bar, add 2 tablespoons of finely ground oatmeal or coffee. For sensitive skin, omit essential oils. Store in a cool, dry place. In Africa, many makers add a few drops of tea tree oil for its antibacterial properties. Always test a small batch first. If the bar is too soft, reduce the water or add more shea butter. If too hard, add a little more coconut oil. This basic bar is gentle enough for face and body, but avoid using on broken skin. Wrap in paper or cloth to preserve freshness. Label with ingredients and date.

lessons.title: Making Liquid Black Soap: Formulation and Preservation
lessons.body: Liquid black soap is made by dissolving raw black soap in water. Use a 1:3 ratio: 100g of grated black soap to 300ml of distilled or boiled (cooled) water. You will need a large pot, a whisk, a thermometer, and a preservative such as Germall Plus or Optiphen (at 0.5-1% of total weight). Start by bringing water to a boil, then remove from heat. Add the grated soap and whisk gently until dissolved. Let it sit for 1 hour, then whisk again. If lumps remain, strain through a fine mesh or cheesecloth. The mixture will be thick; adjust consistency by adding more water. For a smoother liquid, use a stick blender for 30 seconds. Now add preservative: for 500ml of liquid soap, add 2.5-5ml of preservative. Stir well. Without preservative, liquid soap grows mold within days. You can also add 10ml of glycerin for moisture and 5ml of essential oil (like lavender or tea tree) for scent. Pour into clean bottles. Label with date. Shelf life is 6-12 months if preserved. To use: shake well, apply to wet skin or hair, lather, and rinse. For a thicker shampoo, reduce water to 200ml. For a body wash, add 1 tablespoon of honey. In Africa, many makers use local lemongrass or eucalyptus oil. Always test pH; ideal is 8-9. If too alkaline, add a few drops of citric acid solution. Never use metal containers; use glass or plastic. Store away from sunlight.

lessons.title: Developing Black Soap Scrubs with Local Exfoliants (e.g., Coffee, Sugar)
lessons.body: To make a black soap scrub, start with 200g of raw black soap, grated. Add 100g of exfoliant: used coffee grounds (dried), brown sugar, or fine sea salt. For coffee scrub, use 50g of coffee grounds and 50g of sugar. You also need 50ml of carrier oil (coconut, olive, or shea oil), 10ml of vitamin E oil, and 5ml of essential oil (optional). In a bowl, mix the grated soap with the exfoliant. Add the carrier oil and mix until it forms a paste. If too dry, add 1 tablespoon of warm water. If too wet, add more exfoliant. For a finer scrub, grind the coffee grounds or sugar in a blender. For a coarser scrub, leave as is. Scoop into jars. This recipe makes about 300g. Use within 4 weeks if kept in a cool, dry place; refrigeration extends to 8 weeks. To use: apply a small amount to wet skin, massage in circles for 30 seconds, then rinse. Do not use on face if you have acne; use a gentler sugar scrub. For face, use 100g soap, 50g fine sugar, 30ml jojoba oil. For body, use coffee for cellulite and circulation. In Africa, many add moringa powder or baobab fruit powder for extra nutrients. Always patch test. Avoid getting water into the jar. If the scrub separates, stir before use. Label with ingredients and date. This scrub is excellent for rough knees, elbows, and feet.

lessons.title: Formulating Black Soap Shampoo and Conditioner
lessons.body: For black soap shampoo, mix 100g of liquid black soap (from Module 5 Lesson 2) with 50ml of aloe vera gel, 20ml of coconut oil, and 10ml of vegetable glycerin. Add 5ml of tea tree oil for dandruff or 5ml of peppermint oil for stimulation. Stir well. Pour into a bottle. This shampoo cleanses without stripping natural oils. For a conditioner, mix 100ml of shea butter (melted) with 50ml of coconut oil, 20ml of honey, and 10ml of vitamin E oil. Whip with a hand mixer for 5 minutes until fluffy. Add 5ml of lavender oil for scent. Store in a jar. To use shampoo: wet hair, apply 2 tablespoons, massage scalp, rinse. Follow with conditioner: apply a small amount to ends, leave 5 minutes, rinse. For dry hair, add 10ml of castor oil to the shampoo. For oily hair, reduce coconut oil to 10ml and add 10ml of lemon juice. In Africa, many use black soap shampoo for locs and natural hair. It removes buildup and promotes growth. Adjust pH to 5.5-6.5 with citric acid solution if needed. Without preservative, use within 2 weeks; with preservative, 6 months. Always test on a small section first. For a leave-in conditioner, mix 50ml of conditioner with 100ml of water in a spray bottle. Shake before use. Label with date and ingredients.

lessons.title: Blending Black Soap with Shea Butter for Moisturizing Creams
lessons.body: To make a moisturizing black soap cream, you need 100g of raw black soap (finely grated), 100g of unrefined shea butter, 50ml of coconut oil, 30ml of sweet almond oil, and 10ml of vitamin E oil. Also, 5ml of essential oil (like frankincense or myrrh) optional. Melt shea butter and coconut oil in a double boiler. Remove from heat. Add the grated black soap and stir until dissolved. If the mixture is grainy, use a stick blender for 1 minute. Add sweet almond oil and vitamin E. Stir. Pour into jars. Let it set at room temperature for 4 hours. This cream is thick and rich. For a lighter cream, reduce shea butter to 50g and add 50ml of aloe vera gel. For eczema, add 10ml of neem oil. For acne, add 5ml of tea tree oil. To use: apply a small amount to clean skin morning and night. Massage in circles. For face, use a pea-sized amount. For body, use more. This cream is excellent for dry, ashy skin. In Africa, many add baobab oil or moringa oil. Shelf life is 3 months without preservative; 9 months with 1% Optiphen. Store in a cool, dark place. If it melts in heat, stir and refrigerate for 30 minutes. Always patch test. Do not use on broken skin. Label with ingredients and date. This cream can also be used as a hair butter.

lessons.title: Creating Black Soap Masks and Treatments for Acne and Eczema
lessons.body: For an acne mask, mix 2 tablespoons of raw black soap (grated) with 1 tablespoon of honey, 1 teaspoon of turmeric powder, and 1 teaspoon of tea tree oil. Add 1 tablespoon of water to form a paste. Apply to clean face, avoiding eyes. Leave 10-15 minutes. Rinse with warm water. Use 2-3 times a week. For eczema, mix 2 tablespoons of black soap with 1 tablespoon of colloidal oatmeal, 1 tablespoon of shea butter, and 1 teaspoon of chamomile oil. Apply to affected areas, leave 15 minutes, rinse. For a spot treatment, mix 1 teaspoon of black soap with 1 teaspoon of apple cider vinegar. Dab on pimples, leave 5 minutes, rinse. For a soothing bath soak, add 50g of grated black soap and 100g of Epsom salt to warm bath. Soak 20 minutes. For a scalp treatment for eczema, mix 2 tablespoons of liquid black soap with 1 tablespoon of neem oil. Massage into scalp, leave 30 minutes, rinse. Always patch test. For acne, do not scrub; use gentle circular motions. For eczema, avoid hot water. In Africa, many use moringa leaf powder for its anti-inflammatory properties. Store masks in the fridge for up to 5 days. Make small batches. If irritation occurs, stop use. For severe acne or eczema, see a dermatologist. These treatments complement, not replace, medical care. Label with date and ingredients.
